The protest coincided with a broader day of youth-led demonstrations across Europe, with rallies also unfolding in Rome, Frankfurt and London. While local grievances differed, young crowds voiced shared anger at political leaders whom they accused of sidelining their generation’s priorities amid rising military expenditure and mounting global challenges.

items.titel: Von Prag bis London: Die Jugend geht auf die Strasse
items.anriss: Junge Menschen protestieren gegen Aufrüstung und Krieg und setzen sich für eine lebenswerte Zukunft ein.

absaetze.t: In ganz Europa gingen am Freitag die jungen Menschen auf die Strasse.
Sie demonstrierten gegen Aufrüstung und Krieg und forderten dafür mehr Mittel für Bildung und Klimapolitik.
Zum internationalen Streiktag hatte die europaweite Studierenden- und Jugendbewegung «Youthstrike» aufgerufen.

In mehreren europäischen Städten kam es am Freitag zu grossangelegten Demonstrationen. Die Anliegen der Jungen glichen sich länderübergreifend. Sie forderten mehr Investitionen in die Bildung, ein bezahlbares Leben und mehr Klimaschutz.
Europas Jugend geht auf die Strasse
Sie kritisierten die Aufrüstung und Militarisierung der Länder.
«Gen Z regelt» in Deutschland

In Deutschland kam es am Freitag landesweit zu Protesten, aufgerufen durch die Bewegung «Gen Z regelt». Die Organisatoren der Proteste hatten sich gegen Gewalt verwahrt, die Polizei hatte sich trotzdem für mögliche Krawalle gerüstet.

In Berlin beteiligten sich der Polizei zufolge etwa 4000 Menschen an einem friedlichen Protestzug von «Gen Z regelt». Die Initiative selbst sprach von bis zu 15'000 Demonstranten. Zu einer separaten Kundgebung der Bundesschülerkonferenz am Brandenburger Tor waren 5000 Teilnehmer angemeldet, es kamen aber nur rund 80.

Unter demselben Motto «Schulstreik gegen Wehrpflicht» wurde auch andernorts demonstriert, so etwa in Hamburg, Bremen und Köln. Die Veranstalter von «Schulstreik gegen Wehrpflicht» sprachen von 50'000 protestierenden Schülerinnen und Schülern in 100 Städten – eine Zahl, die schwer überprüfbar war.

In Wien demonstrierten rund 2000 Menschen auf Aufruf einer breiten Koalition linker Organisationen unter dem Motto «Unsere Zukunft statt ihrer Kriege». Sie prangerten die Erhöhung der Militärausgaben an und forderten, dass öffentliche Mittel vorrangig für Wohnraum, Bildung und den Kampf gegen den Klimawandel eingesetzt werden.
Grossstreik in Italien

In Italien demonstrierten Zehntausende Menschen in Rom in drei Demonstrationszügen, darunter einer auf Aufruf der Gewerkschaft CGIL, die von rund hundert Demonstrationen im ganzen Land berichtete, an denen sich über eine Million Menschen beteiligten.

Die Demonstranten protestierten gegen die Aufrüstung, die Lebenshaltungskosten und forderten einen Wandel in der Wirtschafts- und Sozialpolitik der Regierung. Rund tausend Gymnasiasten waren bei dem Protest ebenfalls dabei.
Auch in Mailand marschierten mehrere Zehntausend Demonstranten.

Laut einem Bericht der Nachrichtenagentur Ansa kam es in Bologna zu Zusammenstössen zwischen Demonstranten und der Polizei. Auch aus anderen Städten berichteten lokale Medien von Spannungen bei den Protestaktionen der Studierenden.

In London und Madrid gingen Hunderte Menschen auf die Strasse: In Grossbritannien skandierten die Demonstrierenden unter Polizeischutz «Kämpft für unsere Zukunft, nicht für ihre Kriege», während in der spanischen Hauptstadt gegen höhere Militärausgaben und für das öffentliche Bildungswesen protestiert wurde.

items.titel: Air Force issues massive $16B contract for engine work to dozens of companies
items.anriss: A Pentagon notice said 58 companies were selected to participate in a broad contract for “advanced propulsion enterprise work” through 2041.

absaetze.t: WASHINGTON — The Air Force today named dozens of companies as awardees for a group contract potentially worth $16.1 billion over the next 15 years for “advanced propulsion enterprise work” — though the winners are only seeing a small fraction of that to start.
The contract, announced today, was issued to a total of 58 vendors, who have each been awarded $1,000. The expected work period could stretch to November 2041.
“This contract provides for the continuing enhancement of propulsion technology across all areas and lifecycle phases of propulsion development,” the contract award reads.

The Air Force earlier this year revealed the opportunity for the large contract vehicle, outlining an “Advanced Propulsion Acquisition Contract” in industry solicitations. But a March notice stated the service had not yet secured funding for the initiative, and would not issue contracts until doing so, according to Air & Space Forces Magazine.

Another notice, also posted in March, said the initiative is meant to “enable[] a rapid response applicable to all areas and lifecycle phases of propulsion development, including technology maturation, concept development, concept demonstrations, integration, procurement, production, fielding, operations, and sustainment to quickly meet current and future propulsion system requirements, while maximizing the use of the digital environment.”
The Air Force did not immediately respond to a request for comment seeking further clarity on the contract’s funding and expected scope of work.

The contract’s awardees encompass a range of firms, from startups to established engine primes, who the notice says were each competitively picked. Structured as an indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity contract, the Air Force is not necessarily obligated to spend the full amount.

The award comes as the Air Force seeks new and more effective ways to power its existing and future platforms, from drone wingmen to large mobility aircraft. The service has recently tapped several vendors to open up options for different sizes of drones and missiles, and is also developing an advanced engine that could power future platforms like the F-47 stealth fighter.

items.titel: For a fresh, sunny perspective, focus on what’s behind the camera
items.anriss: Coffee with a photographer. He does lots of work for hotels: some of the best in the world. We get talking about a grand property that we both know, which charges many thousands of euros a night in sunny peak season. He was recently asked …

absaetze.t: Coffee with a photographer. He does lots of work for hotels: some of the best in the world. We get talking about a grand property that we both know, which charges many thousands of euros a night in sunny peak season. He was recently asked to shoot it but, when he sent in his proposal, the general manager called in a panic to say that there had been a misunderstanding. “We don’t pay for these shoots. We let you post the pictures on your Instagram account. It’s good for your reputation.” Yikes. Have hotels learned a few tricks from the blagging influencers who ruin many a poolside moment with their pouts and poses? Personally, I’d prefer less reputation, more cash. Oh, he declined the offer.

I have a camera. It has taken me an age to understand its temperamental ways. If the light is flat or the sky a sullen grey, the device barely makes an effort to help me out, gets properly grumpy. My phone’s camera, however, just soldiers on, pushes through, gets a result no matter what. But if the evening arrives with a golden glow, then it’s a delight to spend time with my little fixed-lens contraption.

I was in Palma last weekend and, on Saturday, I awoke to a perfect day: blue skies, soft autumn light, long shadows. So I picked up my camera, drove down to the coast and walked, with no other mission than to take some pictures. Because there’s something about looking through that viewfinder that helps me to see things better. To take things in. To find focus in so many senses. I might come home with just a handful of pictures that I think are OK but I now embrace the camera’s capriciousness. I find perfection in the imperfections. Photography and a good life have a lot in common.

A friend, a successful architect, invited me to dinner at his house this week. There were two other guests: an artist and maker from Texas, now living in London, and a woman who owns a factory that makes tiles. We ate in the kitchen as William cooked a giant seabass. There was a record player. Nice wine. Most strikingly, though, I don’t remember the last time that I was at a dinner where no phones were in sight, not even to quickly look something up. And I mean this as the greatest compliment: it was an easy dinner. I stress too much about these gatherings, feeling the need to make a pudding and numerous courses, so I usually end up booking a restaurant. But some nice ice cream, cheese and more wine meant that there was time to talk – and listen. To focus in.

An encounter this week made me think that perhaps some people have a natural lens finder always attached to their eye. I went to meet a tailor and, though he had a tape measure draped around his neck, he barely needed it. With his eye alone, he knew the width of a shoulder, the size of a waist. I watched his face. He was mocking up the finished product in his head. He saw things that others would never spot. It has been a week of finding focus.

items.titel: Is GTA VI the Art Miami Deserves?
items.anriss: “Driving at rush hour. SIGNIFICANTLY less cars on the road.” The text was from Miami-based artist, educator, and organizer misael soto, sent yesterday, November 19, a few hours after the release of Grand Theft Auto VI . We’d come full …

absaetze.t: Miami-based artists Leo Castañeda and misael soto join Hyperallergic in a conversation about the tensions of a game that portrays a changing city locked in time.
November 20, 2026 — 17 min read

“Driving at rush hour. SIGNIFICANTLY less cars on the road.” The text was from Miami-based artist, educator, and organizer misael soto, sent yesterday, November 19, a few hours after the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. We’d come full circle: The bumper-to-bumper traffic that Miami, the city I once called home, is now notorious for — in no small part due to overdevelopment, climate change, and strained infrastructure — was being alleviated by a video game that keeps people at home, inside a simulation of the same city locked in time.

The premise of GTA VI is simple on the surface. The game follows Lucía Caminos and Jason Duval in the criminal underworld of Leonida, a fictionalized state based on South Florida: Miami becomes Vice City, the Everglades are the Grassrivers. But its portrayal of real-life hardships, socioeconomic inequality, and even Lucía and Jason’s love story, among other elements, has elicited deeper reflections and responses across our increasingly blurred online and physical worlds.

To help make sense of these tensions, I got on a phone call with soto and Leo Castañeda, two Miami-based artists whose work I admire. Castañeda is an artist and video game designer exploring Latin American Surrealism in the digital age, and soto co-leads Artists for Artists: Miami, which is leading a boycott of Art Basel next month, and works in the overlapping arenas of labor rights, public infrastructure, and conceptual and social practice.
Our conversation was edited and condensed for clarity. I hope you enjoy it.
Hyperallergic: Before we even get into GTA, I was hoping each of you could tell me a little bit about your relationship to Miami — how long you've been there? How do you feel about living there now?

Leo Castañeda: I moved to Miami first when I was 11. My parents first moved to New York [from Colombia], and then they thought it was too cold, so they moved to Miami. I went to middle school and high school here, then I moved to New York for college, and I moved back in 2015. When I first moved back after college, it was mostly because of the cost of living in New York. And then, within the 10 years that I've been here, it became the same cost of living as New York, except with Florida salaries.

I do feel grateful, though, to be part of the Bakehouse Art Complex, where I have an affordable studio. I live in the North Beach area, and I was able to find a sustainable rent. Miami has a lot of arts nonprofits that help over time. I do feel that, as complicated as the Miami arts ecosystem is, it is pretty supportive — but at the same time, it is tied to all the different layers of money that have come in and dominate the arts, which are very present here.

misael soto: I moved here right after undergrad. I grew up in South Florida, originally from Puerto Rico, and Miami was always la locura, down south. We would visit my cousins and whatnot from time to time. As I became more and more interested in starting my own practice, I moved down here and have continually been sucked back in. I try to leave, and it pulls me back for whatever reason. Since COVID, everything's changed. Miami became the second most expensive city in the country. The influx was palpable: All of a sudden, there were Texas and California and New York license plates, Teslas zipping around town, and rent just started skyrocketing. There's more flooding. But at the same time, it's gorgeous, and it's special. I live in Mid-Beach. I can go to the water, I can breathe in some sea air, I can hear 10 different languages at once.

It's a really complex relationship with Miami. Especially, I think, both of us make complicated art — we both make art that is unconventional and perhaps even, you could say, difficult to collect. I don't know if you describe yourself that way, Leo, but I definitely do. And making this kind of work in a hyper market-driven neoliberal city like Miami, on the one hand, it gives me a lot of fodder, a lot of material, a lot of things to talk about, as we're doing right now. But at the same time, it can be really frustrating and alienating and lonesome, ultimately.

H: I moved from Argentina to Miami when I was little because my mom got a job there. We lived in the Doral neighborhood, where most people I knew were also from Latin America, until I left for Chicago for college at 18. I've lived in New York for over a decade now, but I still feel a strong pull to Miami, I feel seen, surrounded by people whose identities are a bit fractured the way I feel mine is.

And on the note of nostalgia, GTA is a game that was made over the last 13 years, so it chronicles a Miami that’s partly gone. For example, users say Lucía's home is based on a cute salmon-pink, 13-unit condo in Edgewater that was demolished in 2022 to build a 55-story tower, yet it lives on in the game. What does it mean for a video game to preserve a place that no longer exists?

LC: Well, a few thoughts. During that 13-year development, I would assume the map design was one of the first things they did. But there are also aspects of the chronicling of Miami, or Miami becoming this satire through the game, that have evolved in a shorter time period. For example, this morning I woke up, and there was a Miami Instagram influencer saying that in the fictional version of the Cuban coffee shop Versailles, which is called Antoinette, the bakery has a sign posted outside that says something like, “any politician must pay for all the food when they leave.” That's a reference from a few years ago, when Trump reportedly went to Versailles, ordered food for everyone, and then didn't pay and just walked out.

So it does seem like a video game takes a long time to make, and this one is probably the most ambitious one ever made — 4,500 people working really, really hard, to the point of even having the union situations that they have in the UK branch of the company. But at the same time, I feel like they studied Miami extremely well, and the integration with some local businesses and local artists in particular — I've seen a few street artists like Ahol Sniffs Glue, Soak, Tatiana Suarez, Typoe, as well as musician Nick León. One restaurant is based on Juvia on Lincoln Road, which doesn't exist anymore — they got priced out, and now there's a record of it. The game takes so long to make, but it lives in an ever-present, because it doesn't matter if you made an asset 13 years in the past, like Lucía's apartment, or now; they feel like the present. It's an interesting amalgamation. I would have to spend more time with it to really know: Does this feel like Miami in 2014 or Miami in 2026, or a hybrid?

H: To get into the politics of the conversation around GTA, I have a lot of icky feelings about one narrative that's taking hold online, which is that the game is “Woke 3.0,” and that the incels and Trump supporters are pissed about it. I only played for a few hours last night, and I went into a gun shop and bought a shotgun. That, to me, panders much more to the NRA hawks and the pro-gun community than to anything that could be considered woke, you know?

MS: Hmm. I see it the other way around, actually. To me, it's like pretending in order to pacify, in some ways. It's a very complex thing. On the one hand, I remember seeing the woman twerking on the top of a car as the sun came up over the MacArthur. Now that's in the game. And I remember the “face eater” on the MacArthur. I see a man in a thong skateboarding weekly, and now there's a character like that in the game. I teach art history, and I do a whole week on postmodernism and poststructuralism and simulacrum, and the consequences of that, which I think have led us into some really dangerous flattening territory in terms of the role of the artist in the late 20th to early 21st century. I see this game and the way that it's taken over the city in real life and in gameplay, and it makes me think about how much of this is pacifying the role of the artist, or is it pushing through to the other end and becoming a meta-modernist critique that has some gems in there, if you're willing to find them?

It ultimately makes me feel a bit sad in terms of what we deserve. I texted you yesterday, Valentina, when we were talking about having this conversation, and I said, “Well, maybe this is the kind of art the city deserves.” It's not the art that I want for Miami. But in so many ways, Miami is the perfect place. It's been the city for continual use by image makers, from Hollywood to video games.

H: There is some talk about the fact that the game does seem to have an awareness and sensitivity around identity. Cygnus, the curator at the Vice City Museum of Art, is the first non-binary character in Grand Theft Auto history. The actor cast for the role, Jesse James Rose, said that to prevent anti-trans violence, GTA made it so players would not be able to harm their character. Does this feel like an honest gesture, though?

MS: I was just talking to a friend who's been playing it, and she was like, “Where are all the Haitians?” I remembered there was this huge lawsuit against GTA and Vice City, the one set in the ’80s, from about 20 years ago. Haitian groups sued Rockstar over their portrayal. I did some research, and it seems now the company has shifted. They're saying, “We now punch up as opposed to punching down.” That feels, once again, so uncanny in comparison to the ways in which corporate America has shifted. It makes me think of the phrase, “Black faces in high places won't save us.” I don't want to be lobbing grenades at Rockstar. I think it's fantastic that these changes have been made, especially with such an influential game. But at the same time, it feels like the video game, in its attempt to replicate reality, is lagging in this area.

H: GTA has a long history of racism. We shouldn't forget that Black characters have been associated with criminality throughout all editions of the game. I haven't played enough to say whether that's the case in the latest version. There is also the question of how the company actually treats its workers, and the labor disputes that are going on behind the scenes. Nestor Uriarte, an animation programmer for Rockstar, wrote an opinion piece for the Guardian where he asked, why is it that with this game that generated billions of dollars, we are still fighting to get union recognition?

MS: I'm curious, Leo, as someone who has been playing games for as long as you have, how you feel about this. I'm a cinephile — I've been one since I was 18, and watched my first Kubrick film the summer before college. And I am dying to see Avengers: Doomsday (2026). I've been following the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) and have been consistently floored by the way they built out this world and the interconnected films. It's history, and it's been making history. But we all know how terrible Disney is. And even with the MCU, they tried to bring in more diversity, and the public didn't respond, so they backtracked on it. I don't know if that analogy holds. But it feels pertinent. It feels similar.

items.titel: A Sprawling Exhibition of Latin American Art and Fashion Is Coming to NYC
items.anriss: Patricia Belli, Troy Montes Michie, Willy Chavarria, and Camila Falquéz are among the 20 artists and designers who will be featured in Malvestir , MoMA PS1's upcoming exhibition on the visual lexicon of Latin American fashion, opening in …

absaetze.t: Twenty artists and designers across the Americas will be featured in "Malvestir" at MoMA PS1 this spring, probing the historical and contemporary resonances of Latin American dress.
November 20, 2026 — 3 min read

Patricia Belli, Troy Montes Michie, Willy Chavarria, and Camila Falquéz are among the 20 artists and designers who will be featured in Malvestir, MoMA PS1's upcoming exhibition on the visual lexicon of Latin American fashion, opening in April 2027.

A portmanteau of the Spanish words mal (poorly) and vestir (to dress), Malvestir features creatives across the Americas who probe the historical and contemporary resonances of Latin American dress. Western appropriations of Indigenous crafts, exorbitant textile waste, and the fetishization of Latin American styles are just some of the key concerns that will be interrogated in the exhibition.

Curated by MoMA PS1 director Connie Butler and associate curator Elena Ketelsen González, Malvestir will include a range of artists, from New York City designers to textile artists reinvigorating intergenerational weaving traditions.

Several designers are striving to reclaim styles and symbols co-opted by mainstream Western markets. Known for his oversized proportions and street-style designs emblematic of the Mexican-American fashion tradition, New York designer Willy Chavarria is showing Safe From Home (2024), a film that expanded upon themes of love and the right to safety explored in his Autumn/Winter 2024 collection. Malvestir will also include the work of designer Carla Fernández, who nurtures collaborations with local artisans in Mexico to preserve Indigenous motifs against corporate reproduction and profiteering.

Works from multimedia artists who use photography, drawing, painting, sculpture, and textiles to preserve intergenerational customs will also be on view. New Mexico-based artist Josh Tafoya revitalizes his family’s weaving tradition through the centuries-long practice of Rio Grande loom weaving. David Ramirez Cotón pays homage to Guatemalan fashion with a series of hyperrealistic acrylic-on-canvas paintings cut to resemble articles of clothing hanging from a rack in a second-hand shop.

The exhibition comes at a time when Latin American communities are facing regressive crackdowns from multiple parties — the federal government, exploitative corporations, and immigration enforcement. Yet it has also prompted many to recognize the importance of Latinx artists through displaying the full range and power of their respective cultures, as mainstream appropriation and demands for assimilation reach new, threatening extremes.

In an opinion for Hyperallergic this month, Arlene Dávila, a professor of anthropology and American Studies at New York University, positioned the current political climate as a rallying cry for Latinx visionaries.

Within her essay, she referenced Chavarria and Raul Lopez (founder of LUAR), two of the artists whose work will appear in Malvestir, underscoring how they "frequently use street-cast Black and Brown models to communicate a richer, more inclusive vision beyond traditional, Eurocentric runways."

"Across these fields, artists are choosing to create work that is deeply rooted in their communities, drawing directly from vernacular traditions, oral histories, and family memories that were once pushed to the margins," Dávila wrote. "While they recognize there are no guarantees of commercial or institutional rewards, their work stems from a shared conviction: We have rich cultures to offer, and we will tell our stories by any means necessary."

items.titel: Russian strikes damage historic buildings in Kyiv and Odesa, including World Heritage sites
items.anriss: The St Volodymyr’s Cathedral and the St Michael’s Golden-Domed Cathedral and Monastery in Kyiv are among the heritage buildings targeted in recent Russian attacks

absaetze.t: Multiple heritage sites in Ukraine were damaged by Russian strikes on 19 and 20 November, including the Unesco-listed St Michael’s Golden-Domed Cathedral and Monastery complex and St Volodymyr’s Cathedral in Kyiv, known for its frescoes, as well as 12 cultural heritage sites in Odesa, the strategic port city on the Black Sea, which was hit a day earlier. The entire historic centre of Odesa was added to Unesco’s list of endangered World Heritage sites in 2023.
At least nine people were killed in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine during the hours-long attack on 20 November.

“Today, Russian drones damaged one of the most famous monuments of our country, the Volodymyr Cathedral,” Tetyana Berezhna, Ukraine’s deputy prime minister for humanitarian policy and minister of culture, wrote in a Facebook post on 19 November after the cathedral in Kyiv was hit, breaking windows and frames and causing “some damage to the paintings and structural elements”.

The neo-Byzantine St Volodymyr Cathedral, built in the 19th century, is under the jurisdiction of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (OCU), which broke with the Moscow Patriarchate and was granted autocephaly by Constantinople in 2018. Three of Russia’s most famous artists of the 19th century and early 20th century—Viktor Vasnetsov, Mikhail Vrubel and Mikhail Nesterov—created religious art for St Volodymyr’s, as did the Ukrainian artist Mykola Pymomenko, a teacher of Kazimir Malevich.

The Austrian embassy, located next-door to St Volodymyr's Cathedral, was also damaged. Kyiv's municipal cultural heritage department published an inventory of damage from the attack, which also includes the embassy of the Netherlands.
A Russian drone was shot down over St Michael’s, which is the headquarters of the OCU, on 19 November.

Berezhna’s post cites the cumulative damage from Russia’s accelerating attacks: “Since the beginning of this year, the number of monuments damaged by Russia has increased by more than a third, and by the end of October it was almost 2,200. Almost 2,700 cultural institutions were also affected.”

The minister was in Lutsk, a historic city in northwestern Ukraine, this week to plan for a conference marking the 600th anniversary in 2029 of the Congress of Lutsk, which brought together the regional monarchies of the time. A Russian strike on Lutsk in October damaged Ukraine’s largest painting, Cosmogony, a 2,000 sq. m work by the contemporary artist Petro Antyp.

Unesco has condemned the latest attacks, especially on Odesa, “which hit the centre of the city, within the boundaries of the World Heritage property ‘The Historic Centre of Odesa’” and “reportedly caused damage to several heritage buildings, including the Kalio Palace, a monument of national importance,” according to a statement released by the organisation. The Kalio Palace, built in 1834, is attributed to the Swiss Italian architect Giorgio Torricelli.

The strikes came amid escalating tensions and a diplomatic chasm that appears to be widening. The Russian President Vladimir Putin said this week that the Kremlin would not negotiate any partial ceasefire or deal with Ukraine after it struck and incapacitated the Kerch Bridge linking mainland Russia to Crimea, a symbol of Russia’s annexation of the Black Sea peninsula in 2014, on 16 and 17 November. At the same time, US President Donald Trump claimed that peace, largely on Russia’s terms, is within reach and reportedly urged European leaders to stop funding weapons for Ukraine. Trump, Putin and the Chinese President Xi Jinping signed a “peace declaration” on 20 November at a trilateral summit hosted by Xi in Shenzhen, China.

A petition to “safeguard Ukraine’s cultural heritage and artistic integrity” was launched last month by the curator Konstantin Akinsha and Bjorn Geldof, the artistic director at Kyiv’s PinchukArtCentre. It calls “for immediate sanctions and the suspension of Russian state participation in international cultural events”. Rapporteur, a Brussels-based policy publication, reported this week that ten European countries are seeking to keep Russia out of the 2027 Architecture Biennale. Russia’s participation in the 2026 Venice Biennale set off a series of protests.
